articles.title: Microsoft’s Agent 365 tackles multicloud AI governance
articles.description: For more than 20 years, I have watched cloud computing evolve from a relatively simple extension of enterprise infrastructure into a distributed collection of platforms, services, data stores, applications, and now AI agents. One lesson has remained clear: Enterprises don’t operate in the clean, single-vendor environments that providers portray in their marketing. They operate in heterogeneous environments. They always have. A company that has standardized on one public cloud for core infrastructure might use another for a specialized data platform, rely on Salesforce for customer engagement, run analytics in Databricks or Snowflake, and deploy dozens of software-as-a-service applications throughout the business. Add the current explosion of AI models, agent platforms, developer tools, and local AI clients, and the need for unified management becomes much more urgent. This is what makes Microsoft’s Agent 365 announcement so significant. Microsoft is positioning Agent 365 as a common control plane for managing, governing, securing, and measuring the value of AI agents across both Microsoft and non-Microsoft platforms. It’s more than another cost dashboard; it acknowledges that multicloud is now the standard operating model for most enterprises. It’s also a refreshingly practical position from a company that has historically built some of the industry’s most successful proprietary technology ecosystems. Enterprises are heterogeneous The biggest disconnect in cloud computing has often been between what providers want customers to do and what customers actually need to do. Providers prefer that enterprises consolidate around their platforms. It makes commercial sense. A larger footprint means more consumption, stronger customer retention, and a better opportunity to sell adjacent services. However, enterprise architecture doesn’t work that way. Different business units make different technology decisions. Acquisitions introduce new systems. Developers select tools based on productivity. Data teams choose platforms based on performance and capabilities. Security groups adopt products that fit their risk models. In many cases, the best technology decision for a particular workload is not the best technology decision for the entire company. The result is a hybrid and multicloud environment that must be governed as a whole. AI increases that complexity. Organizations manage more than virtual machines, containers, databases, and APIs. They also manage AI agents that can access corporate data, invoke services, make decisions, and take action. A sales organization may use Salesforce agents. A software engineering group may use GitHub Copilot and Claude Code. A data organization may build agents on Databricks or Snowflake. Other teams may work with Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, OpenAI, or Anthropic. No serious enterprise will limit itself to one AI platform simply to make a vendor’s management tools easier to use. A common control plane is a win The core value proposition of Agent 365 is straightforward: a common management layer for Microsoft and supported non-Microsoft agents. That includes inventory, identity, risk assessment, policy controls, activity monitoring, and cost and value analytics. This is the approach enterprises need. Cloud cost management and observability tools have long been extensions of proprietary platforms, working well for workloads in one provider’s environment but less effectively across competing clouds and SaaS platforms. That leaves customers with an uncomfortable choice: accept incomplete visibility and manage each provider separately, or buy third-party tools and spend time integrating data across multiple systems. Neither option is ideal. Agent 365 recognizes that the control plane should reflect the enterprise estate and not the provider’s product catalog. Microsoft is extending visibility and governance across platforms such as Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Salesforce Agentforce, Databricks, Snowflake, Anthropic, OpenAI, Oracle, SAP, ServiceNow, UiPath, and others. The level of integration will differ across platforms, as it always does in cross-vendor environments. Still, the strategic direction is important. Microsoft is choosing to govern the enterprise as it exists rather than insisting that the enterprise conform to Microsoft’s preferred architecture. AI cost management The finops aspect of Agent 365 may be the most immediately useful feature for many organizations. AI costs are rising quickly, and most companies still lack standard ways to connect AI spending to measurable business outcomes. That problem should sound familiar to anyone who has worked with cloud economics. Early cloud cost management focused heavily on infrastructure utilization, reserved capacity, tagging, and monthly spend. Those necessary operational disciplines are not enough. Business leaders eventually want to know whether the spending is justified. AI introduces the same challenge at a faster pace. It is easy to measure tokens, model calls, inference volume, and subscription costs. It is much harder to determine whether an AI agent is completing useful work, reducing manual effort, improving customer outcomes, or generating enough value to justify continued investment. Agent 365 Business Analytics seeks to connect AI spend with usage and value indicators such as assisted hours, success rates, satisfaction, and specific use cases. That is a more mature direction than simply reporting what each service costs. Of course, organizations should remember that no dashboard can perfectly calculate business value. Productivity metrics can be misleading when they aren’t tied to real business outcomes. Companies need to validate their assumptions, understand how metrics are calculated, and avoid overstating ROI based on early usage data. The effort to connect costs to outcomes is exactly where enterprise AI management needs to go. A smart strategic shift For much of its history, Microsoft built enormous value through tightly integrated, proprietary platforms. Windows, Office, SQL Server, Active Directory, and many other products succeeded in part because they offered customers a cohesive stack. That strategy was not wrong. It created useful technology and delivered real operational advantages. But the cloud changed the rules. Azure’s success depended on Microsoft becoming more open, more interoperable, and more willing to meet customers where they were. Linux support, open source investments, Kubernetes, cross-platform development tools, and hybrid cloud management all reflected this shift. Agent 365 follows the same logic. Microsoft recognizes that it can create more value by managing a diverse AI ecosystem than by requiring every AI workload to run exclusively on Microsoft technology. This approach positions Microsoft at the center of AI operations, even when a competitor provides the underlying agent, model, data platform, or cloud service. That’s a smart place to be. The real test is execution The promise of Agent 365 is compelling, but its execution will matter more than the announcement. Cross-platform management is difficult. Each provider exposes different data, identity models, policy mechanisms, billing structures, APIs, and telemetry levels. A unified dashboard is useful, but only if the data is consistent enough to support meaningful decisions. Governance is useful, but only if organizations can reliably enforce policies where they matter. Enterprises should evaluate Agent 365 based on the specific tools and platforms they use. They should ask whether the product provides inventory, activity monitoring, cost visibility, risk information, identity integration, and enforcement capabilities at the depth they require. They should also understand which features are generally available, which remain in preview, and where platform-specific limitations apply. That said, Microsoft deserves credit for taking the lead in its architectural position. For the past two decades, I have advised organizations to design for heterogeneity because heterogeneity is inevitable. Multicloud is not a failure of strategy; it is the reality produced by diverse business needs, distributed technology decisions, and rapid innovation. Microsoft’s Agent 365 recognizes that reality. Rather than confining itself to a single vendor’s proprietary ecosystem, it’s an observability tool that offers a common control plane that can span Microsoft and non-Microsoft AI platforms. Enterprise cloud customers need more vendors to think like this. Well done, Microsoft.

articles.title: Australian rare earths explorer Barkly delivers five-fold increase in inferred MRE
articles.description: ASX-listed rare earths explorer Barkly Rare Earths has released an updated inferred mineral resource estimate (MRE) of 205-million tonnes grading 2 100 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxide (TREO) for 420 000 t of contained TREO for the Barkly project in Australia's Northwest Territories. The updated MRE has a five-fold increase in tonnage at similar grades to the prior inferred MRE, incorporating 98 new drillholes.
